role: Design management and envelope, with Cade (Digital design and BIM)
title: Design Management: The Owner Decides What, the Team Decides How
summary: Design management is the owner's control system for the design phase: a written brief, defined stages, a gate at the end of each stage, consultant scopes with no gaps between them, a coordinated model and a clear statement of how the finished building must perform. Get it right and most construction surprises never happen.
body:
The cheapest moment to change a building is before it is drawn, and the most expensive is after it is built. Design management is the owner's discipline for making decisions at the cheap end: a clear brief, stage gates you actually hold, consultant scopes that leave no gaps, and a written statement of how the building must perform.

Recall

Q. What is a voidable transfer, in concept?

A. A transfer of assets a court may reverse because it was made to defeat creditors or left the transferor unable to pay known debts. Tests and time limits vary by jurisdiction.

Q. What are the four quiet faults that destroy personal wealth?

A. Currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan, which tend to arrive together in a crisis.

Q. In a trust, who holds legal title and who benefits?

A. The trustee holds legal title and owes duties to the beneficiaries, who hold the benefit. The settlor creates the trust.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week opens the phase on designing the building. As a developer you will not draw, calculate or model. You will decide what the building must be, approve each stage, and pay for the consequences of every gap between consultants. Most cost overruns and disputes on site were set in motion during design, usually by a decision made late, a scope nobody owned, or a drawing that did not match another. Your control over all three is design management.

The brief and the stages

In plain English, the brief is the owner's written statement of what the building is for: who uses it, how many units of what size, the quality level, the budget, the programme, and how it must perform. Everything the designers produce is tested against it.

In American practice, design usually moves through recognisable stages: programming or pre-design, schematic design, design development and construction documents, followed by permitting, bidding and construction administration. Each stage adds detail and fixes more decisions. The professional framing is that the brief should mature with the stages. Early on it states needs and limits; by design development it should be firm enough that changing it means a formal change with a cost.

Cade adds the digital side. On most serious projects, the design is built as a coordinated three-dimensional model, with each discipline's model combined so that clashes, such as a duct passing through a beam, can be found on screen rather than on site. Building information modelling, usually called BIM, and clash detection get their own lessons later this week. Today the point is that the model is a design management tool, not a drawing aid.

Stage gates

A stage gate is a formal review at the end of a stage, where the owner decides whether the design is ready to move forward. The gate checks the design against the brief, the cost estimate against the budget, the schedule against the programme, open risks and unresolved coordination. The decision is one of three: proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.

Worked example one, hypothetical. At the end of schematic design, the cost consultant estimates 32,000,000 dollars against a budget of 30,000,000. The architect wants to move to design development and find savings later. At the gate you decide: proceed with conditions, requiring a costed list of savings totalling at least 2,000,000 within four weeks, before design development drawings for the affected areas begin. Finding 2,000,000 at schematic stage may mean simplifying the massing or the structural grid. Finding it in construction documents means redrawing coordinated work across every discipline.

Say that out loud now.

A gate I do not hold is not a gate. Proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.

Consultant scopes and the gaps between them

A building is designed by many firms: architect, structural, mechanical, electrical and plumbing engineers, civil, landscape, fire protection, envelope, lighting, acoustics, elevators and others. Each signs a scope. The danger is not that a scope is wrong; it is that something falls between two scopes and nobody designs it.

The control is a responsibility matrix: a table listing every element of the building down one side and every consultant across the top, with one name responsible for each element and others marked as contributing. Common gaps include roof drainage at the envelope edge, firestopping of service penetrations, supports for heavy equipment, waterproofing at below-grade transitions and coordination of ceiling space.

Worked example two, hypothetical. The matrix shows the façade engineer designs the curtain wall, the structural engineer designs the slab edge, and nobody is listed for the brackets connecting the two. That single blank cell could later become a dispute, a delay and a redesign during construction. Filling it now costs a sentence in one consultant's scope and perhaps a modest additional fee.

Commissioning intent: the owner's project requirements

The brief says what the building is; the owner's project requirements say how it must perform. Temperature and humidity ranges, ventilation, energy targets, backup power expectations, acoustic limits, maintenance access. The design team responds with a basis of design explaining how its systems meet them. Commissioning, the testing of systems at the end, then tests against the same document. The commissioning process is described in industry guidance from ASHRAE; verify against the current edition before relying on its detail. If the requirements are never written, the building is tested against nothing.

How the best do it

Large, experienced owners and contractors tend to share several design-management habits. They write a performance-focused brief before appointing consultants. They hold formal gate reviews with a cost check at each. They run regular combined model coordination meetings, with clashes tracked to closure. And they bring constructability reviewers, people who will build it, into design early. A small developer can copy the brief, the gates, the matrix and one constructability review per stage without a large team.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the late decision: the owner who keeps the brief open to keep options alive, and keeps changing it into construction documents. Every late change ripples through every coordinated discipline. The control is a dated brief freeze at the end of design development, with any later change going through formal change control and a cost.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the architect manages everything and that a full consultant team means a full scope. It does not. Each firm designs what its contract says. The owner must make sure the contracts together cover the whole building.

A second beginner's mistake is approving drawings by looking at them. A drawing can look complete and still disagree with the structural drawings, the brief or the budget. Approve against the checklist for the gate: brief compliance, cost, schedule, open coordination items and the responsibility matrix, each signed off by the person who checked it.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax: design and development costs may be capitalised or deducted differently, and the treatment should be confirmed; verify against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: consultant contracts, insurance and scope define who carries the risk of a design error. Banking: lenders and their monitors will ask for the design status, the estimate and the permit path before funding. Governance: write down who may approve a gate or a change. Estate: design contracts and models are assets and obligations of the project company and must pass with it. Exit: a building designed for maintenance and durability is worth more to its next owner.

Callback

In week 49, Marco and Quincy taught scope, the work breakdown structure and change control for construction. Design has the same anatomy. The responsibility matrix is the design phase's work breakdown structure, and the brief freeze is the point at which design changes start being priced as change orders.

Recap

Design management is a written brief, defined stages, gates you hold, consultant scopes with no gaps, a coordinated model and written performance requirements. Decide early, freeze the brief, and price every later change.

Next: Ford, on Failure Forensics: the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and a design change nobody owned.
checklist: I have a written brief that states use, size, quality, budget, programme and performance.
I know which design stage the project is in.
I hold a formal gate at the end of each stage with a cost check.
Each gate ends in proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.
I have a responsibility matrix with one name against every element.
I have written owner's project requirements for system performance.
I freeze the brief at a dated point and route later changes through change control.
I commission one constructability review per stage.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, design management is the owner's control system for the design phase. It starts with a written brief: what the building is for, its size, quality, budget, programme and performance. Design moves through stages, schematic design, design development and construction documents, and at the end of each the owner holds a gate: proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework, with a cost check every time. The biggest hidden risk is the gap between consultants, so I keep a responsibility matrix with one name against every element of the building. The owner's project requirements state how the systems must perform, and commissioning tests against them. Cade's coordinated model finds clashes on screen rather than on site. Decide early, freeze the brief at a dated point, and price every change after that. The cheapest time to change a building is before it is drawn.
terms: Stage gate — a formal owner review at the end of a design stage that decides whether to proceed, proceed with conditions or rework.
Responsibility matrix — a table assigning one responsible consultant to every element of the building.
Owner's project requirements — the owner's written statement of how the building and its systems must perform.

hostile.q: Your cost estimate at schematic design is two million over budget. Why should I keep funding design?
hostile.a: Because I held the gate. Design development is proceeding only on condition that the team delivers a costed savings list of at least two million within four weeks, before the affected areas are developed. If they cannot, the next step is to rework the scheme, not to carry the overrun forward. I can show you the gate record and the condition.

title: The Hyatt Regency Walkways: A Small Change Nobody Owned
summary: On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways in the atrium of the Hyatt Regency Kansas City collapsed during a crowded event, killing 114 people. A hanger detail changed between design and fabrication, and the change was never properly checked. We take it through seven steps and end with a rule about design changes.
body:
The Hyatt Regency walkways did not fail because of an exotic load or an unknown material. They failed because a connection detail changed between the engineer's drawing and the steel fabricator's shop drawing, and nobody took ownership of checking what the change did to the load path.

Recall

Q. In the annual review calculation, which number turned out to be the binding constraint?

A. Severe-case liquidity. Net worth survived the stress case, but usable cash after a guarantee call fell far below the floor.

Q. What was the structural reason the Madoff fraud could last so long?

A. One firm managed, held and reported the money, so there was no independent record to compare against.

Q. What is a discretionary trust?

A. A trust in which the trustee decides which beneficiaries receive what, and when, within the terms of the deed, rather than following fixed entitlements.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, design management is usually taught as cost and schedule. This case is the reason it is also a matter of life and death. As owner you will not check calculations, but you will set up the system that decides who checks changes, how changes are recorded and whether anything can be built to an unchecked detail. The Hyatt case is the clearest lesson there is in what happens when that system fails.

The broad facts come from the public record and the federal investigation that followed. Where I am unsure of a detail I say so.

1. Timeline

The Hyatt Regency Kansas City opened in 1980, with a tall atrium crossed by suspended walkways on the second, third and fourth floors. The second-floor walkway hung directly beneath the fourth-floor walkway. During construction, part of the atrium roof had collapsed [unverified — confirm independently]. On the evening of July 17, 1981, during a crowded tea dance, the fourth- and second-floor walkways fell into the atrium. 114 people died and more than 200 were injured. A federal investigation by the National Bureau of Standards examined the connections. The engineers responsible later lost their engineering licences in Missouri.

2. Key decisions

The original design hung both walkways from continuous steel rods running from the roof structure, through the fourth-floor walkway's beams, down to the second-floor walkway. A continuous rod is hard to fabricate and install over that length. During shop drawing preparation, the steel fabricator proposed replacing each continuous rod with two rods: one from the roof to the fourth-floor beam, and a second from the fourth-floor beam down to the second floor. The shop drawings were returned from the engineer's office approved. The change was built.

3. Assumptions

Each party seems to have assumed another had checked the change. The fabricator assumed the engineer would review the structural effect. The engineer's office treated the shop drawing review as a check of general conformance. Investigators also found that even the original connection fell short of the capacity the building code required, so a design weakness was compounded by a change that made it far worse.

4. Incentives

The fabricator had a legitimate incentive to simplify a hard detail. The engineer's office, reviewing large volumes of shop drawings on a fast schedule, had an incentive to review quickly. Nobody was paid specifically to trace the load path of a proposed change. The incentive structure rewarded progress, not verification.

Say that out loud now.

A change that looks small on a drawing can double the load on a connection. Small is not the same as checked.

5. Warning signs ignored

A proposed change to a primary load-carrying connection. A shop drawing process with unclear responsibility for structural review of fabricator changes. A detail that, as investigators found, was already marginal. And reports during construction that the walkways moved or vibrated when people walked on them [unverified — confirm independently]. Any of these deserved a formal structural check.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the return of the shop drawing marked approved without a calculation. After that, the steel was fabricated and erected to the changed detail, and the building opened. From then on, the connection was waiting for a large enough crowd.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a change-control failure in design. A structural change entered through a fabricator's shop drawing and was accepted without anyone owning the responsibility to recalculate it. Fabrication, review and approval each happened, but the one action that mattered, checking the new load path, belonged to nobody in practice.

The mechanics, in plain terms

Here is why the change mattered, as a hypothetical illustration with round numbers. Call the load from the fourth-floor walkway P, and the load from the second-floor walkway also P. With a continuous rod, the nut under the fourth-floor beam carries only the fourth-floor walkway's load, P, because the second-floor load passes straight up the rod to the roof. With two rods, the second-floor walkway hangs from the fourth-floor beam itself. Now the nut under the fourth-floor beam carries its own walkway plus the walkway below: 2P. The same connection, with the same nut and beam, was asked to carry about twice the load. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.

A second worked example, on cost, hypothetical. Suppose formally recalculating the change, with the engineer's time and a short delay, cost a few thousand dollars and a week. Against that sits the cost of failure, which no number captures. The comparison explains Rule 98 better than any argument.

What the profession took from it

The case is still taught in engineering ethics courses because it is a responsibility failure rather than a calculation failure. The broad lessons the profession drew are worth an owner's attention. The engineer of record remains responsible for the structural integrity of the design, whoever drew the detail. Where a contractor or fabricator designs part of the structure, that delegated design should be explicit, assigned to a licensed engineer, and submitted with calculations. And a shop drawing review stamp should say plainly what was and was not checked.

For you as owner, that becomes three questions to ask at the design development gate. Which connections and components will be designed by the contractor? Who is the licensed engineer for each? And how will a change proposed during fabrication reach the engineer of record before anything is made?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk for an owner is assuming that because a shop drawing is stamped, every change on it has been engineered. The control is to require, in every consultant and contractor contract, that any change to a structural element is identified as a change, submitted with calculations, and approved in writing by the engineer of record before fabrication. The responsibility matrix from lesson 680 should name who reviews delegated and changed connections.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats shop drawings as paperwork between the contractor and the designers. They are where design intent becomes physical steel, and where substitutions enter. The owner does not review them, but the owner decides the rules for how they are reviewed.

Callback

In week 49, Marco and Quincy taught change control in construction: no change is built until it is identified, priced and approved. The Hyatt case is the same principle applied to design, where the price of a change is measured in safety as well as dollars.

The prevention rule

Rule 98: Every change to a structural element after design, including one proposed on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record as a formal, documented change with its own calculation, and nothing is built to it until that check is signed.

Recap

In 1981 two Hyatt Regency walkways fell, killing 114 people, after a hanger detail changed from one continuous rod to two, roughly doubling the load on a connection that was already weak. The change came in on a shop drawing and was never properly recalculated.

Next: Sage, on The Money: how the timing of a design decision moves its cost.
checklist: My contracts require every structural change to be identified as a change.
Every structural change comes with its own calculation.
The engineer of record approves structural changes in writing before fabrication.
My responsibility matrix names who reviews delegated and changed connections.
I know the difference between a conformance review and an engineering check.
Substitutions proposed by fabricators go through the same change process.
I keep a register of every design change with its approval.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, on July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City collapsed during a crowded event, and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods. During shop drawings, the fabricator proposed two shorter rods instead, so the lower walkway hung from the upper walkway's beam. That roughly doubled the load on a connection that investigators found was already short of code capacity. The shop drawings came back approved, but nobody owned the job of recalculating the new load path. Fabrication, review and approval all happened; the one check that mattered did not. The lesson for an owner is about change control in design. Rule 98: every change to a structural element after design, including one proposed on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record with its own calculation, and nothing is built until that check is signed.
terms: Shop drawing — a detailed fabrication drawing prepared by a contractor or fabricator showing how a designed element will be made and installed.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer responsible for the structural design of a project.
Load path — the route by which loads travel through a structure down to the foundations.

hostile.q: The fabricator's change is stamped reviewed. Why are you holding up fabrication for another calculation?
hostile.a: Because a review stamp on a shop drawing is a conformance check, not an engineering check of a change to the load path. The change alters how load passes through a primary connection, so my contract requires the engineer of record to calculate it and approve it in writing before anything is fabricated. If the detail works, the delay is days. If it does not, we have found it on paper.

rule: Rule 98: Every change to a structural element after design, including one proposed on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record as a formal, documented change with its own calculation, and nothing is built to it until that check is signed.

title: When a Design Decision Is Made Decides What It Costs
summary: The same design change costs very little at the brief, more in design development, a great deal in construction documents and the most on site. This lesson prices that curve with hypothetical numbers, shows how coordination and clash detection pay for themselves, and links design fees to the pro forma.
body:
A design decision's cost is set less by what you decide than by when you decide it. Moving a wall at the brief costs an email; moving it after the concrete is poured costs a demolition. Spending on design management is spending to move decisions to the cheap end of that curve.

Recall

Q. In the mock annual review, what did you ask the investment manager before discussing performance?

A. Whether the custodian had changed, whether the custodian's figures matched his, and his total fees including fees inside underlying funds.

Q. How does leverage change the effect of a currency fall on personal equity?

A. It multiplies it, because the whole asset falls with the currency while a debt in another currency does not.

Q. What duties does a trustee owe, in broad terms?

A. To act in the beneficiaries' interests, follow the deed, keep proper accounts, avoid conflicts and make decisions properly and independently.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the pro forma treats design as a soft-cost line, usually a modest share of total cost. That understates its effect. Design decisions set most of the hard cost, the schedule and the operating cost for the building's life. A dollar spent well in design management can protect many dollars of hard cost, and a dollar saved by rushing design can cost many more on site. You need to see that in numbers, not as a slogan.

The cost-of-change curve

In plain English: the later a change, the more work it undoes. Early changes alter ideas. Later changes alter drawings across several disciplines. Changes on site alter built work, and they also stop the work around them.

The professional framing is that the ability to influence cost falls as design progresses, while the cost of making a change rises. The exact shape varies by project; treat any multiplier you see quoted as illustrative, not as a standard.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. The owner decides to move a set of risers to free up a larger unit layout on every floor of a mid-rise building.

StageWhat changesIllustrative cost
BriefA line in the briefClose to nothing
Schematic designPlans redrawn by the architect20,000 dollars
Design developmentArchitecture, structure and services reworked150,000 dollars
Construction documentsCoordinated sets reissued, re-permitting400,000 dollars and weeks of delay
ConstructionBuilt work removed and rebuiltSeveral million dollars and months

The decision is identical in every row. Only its timing changed.

Say that out loud now.

The decision did not change. Only its timing did, and timing set the price.

Clash detection, priced

Cade's contribution is measured the same way. Building information modelling, or BIM, combines each discipline's three-dimensional model into one. Clash detection is software that finds places where two elements occupy the same space, such as a pipe through a beam or a duct through a sprinkler main. Each clash found in the model is a change made at the cheap end.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A model coordination process costs 120,000 dollars across design and preconstruction. It resolves 300 significant clashes. Suppose, as an illustrative assumption for this project, that a third of those, 100 clashes, would otherwise have been found in the field, at an average cost to fix of 5,000 dollars each including lost labour and resequencing. That is 500,000 dollars of avoided field cost, against 120,000 spent. The net saving is 380,000, before counting schedule. The assumption about how many clashes would reach site, and what each would cost, is the number to challenge; the method stands either way.

Translate the saving into the pro forma, still hypothetical. Total development cost is 30,000,000 dollars and stabilised net operating income, or NOI, is 2,000,000 dollars a year. Yield on cost is 2,000,000 divided by 30,000,000, about 6.67 percent. Remove 380,000 of field changes and total cost becomes 29,620,000, so yield on cost rises to about 6.75 percent. That looks small until you remember that the development spread, the gap between yield on cost and the market cap rate, is often only one or two percentage points, so eight hundredths of a point is a real share of the reward for taking development risk.

Now add schedule. Suppose field clashes would also have added one month of delay. If the construction loan is 20,000,000 dollars, nearly fully drawn near completion, at a hypothetical 8 percent a year, one month of interest is about 133,000 dollars, before extra general conditions and a month of lost rent. Schedule is often worth as much as the direct fix, and it is the part owners forget to count.

Design fees and the false economy

Design fees are commercial terms, not standards, often negotiated as a percentage of construction cost or a fixed sum per stage. The beginner's reflex is to squeeze them. Worked example three, hypothetical. On a 40,000,000 dollar building, cutting design fees from 2,400,000 to 2,000,000 saves 400,000. If the cheaper scope drops the coordinated model and one round of constructability review, and that leads to even 1 percent of hard cost in avoidable field changes, the cost is 400,000. The saving has been spent before the building is finished, and the schedule effect is extra.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, a design phase is the period when your equity is most exposed and least liquid: you have bought land and paid designers, and nothing is yet bankable. Warrick's entry records equity committed to design for each project, the date of the next gate, and the amount that would be lost if the project stopped at that gate. Knowing that figure lets you decide whether to proceed with the next stage of spending. A licensed adviser is required before you act on the personal side.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating design as a cost to minimise rather than an investment in fewer changes. The control is to judge design spending by the changes it prevents: require a clash log, a gate cost check and a change register, and look at the trend at each gate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner keeps options open to stay flexible, not realising that each open option is a later change waiting to be priced. Decide, record and freeze.

A related mistake is treating contingency as the place to absorb design changes. Design contingency exists for genuine unknowns that emerge as the design develops, not for decisions the owner postponed. If owner changes are paid from contingency, the contingency is gone by the time the ground or the market produces a real surprise, and the pro forma shows a healthy reserve that no longer exists. Track owner-driven changes on their own line so you can see what your own indecision is costing.

Working with advisers

Designers are advisers, and the same discipline you apply to a wealth manager applies to them. State what you want in writing, ask what is excluded, and ask how they will tell you when they are outside their scope. A good consultant answers those questions without offence.

Then judge them by evidence, not charm: the gate packages, the clash log and the change register. If a consultant's work consistently arrives at the gate unready, that is the conversation to have early, privately and on the record.

Callback

In week 10, Sage taught yield on cost and the development spread. Today's numbers live inside that ratio. Every avoidable change raises cost and narrows the spread between yield on cost and market cap rate, which is the margin that pays you for development risk.

Recap

The cost of a change depends on its timing. Coordination and clash detection pay for themselves when they move changes into the model. Squeezing design fees often buys field changes worth more than the saving.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: the contracts and code duties that govern design.
checklist: I price design changes by the stage they are made in.
I treat published cost multipliers as illustrative, not standards.
I require a combined model and a clash log on serious projects.
I challenge the assumptions behind any claimed coordination saving.
I judge design fees against the field changes they prevent.
I know the equity at risk if a project stops at the next gate.
I keep a change register from the brief freeze onward.
I state each consultant's scope and exclusions in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, a design decision's cost depends mostly on when you make it. In our hypothetical example, moving a set of risers costs almost nothing at the brief, 20,000 dollars at schematic design, 150,000 in design development, 400,000 plus delay in construction documents and several million once built. Same decision; different timing. Clash detection works the same way: combining every discipline's model finds conflicts on screen. If a 120,000 dollar coordination effort keeps 100 clashes out of the field at 5,000 each, it saves 380,000, but challenge the assumption behind that figure. Cutting design fees by 400,000 is a false economy if it drops the model and causes even 1 percent of hard cost in avoidable field changes. On the personal side, know how much equity you lose if the project stops at the next gate. Decide early, record it, and freeze the brief.
terms: Cost-of-change curve — the pattern in which a change costs more the later in design and construction it is made.
Building information modelling (BIM) — designing a building as a coordinated digital model holding geometry and information for every element.
Clash detection — software checking of a combined model to find elements that occupy the same space or conflict.

hostile.q: Your design fees are above the lowest quote. Why should the project pay more for design?
hostile.a: Because the higher fee buys a coordinated model, a clash log and a constructability review at each stage, which move changes to the cheap end of the curve. On my numbers, avoiding even 1 percent of hard cost in field changes repays the difference, and I will report the clash log and change register at every gate so you can see whether it is working.

title: The Contracts and Code Duties Behind a Design
summary: Design is governed by two sets of rules at once: the contracts between the owner and each consultant, and the building code's requirements for who prepares and stands behind construction documents. This lesson explains the standard of care, delegated design, shop drawing responsibility and who owns the drawings and the model.
body:
A design consultant does not promise a perfect building. In most systems, a consultant promises to perform with the care a reasonable professional would use. Everything else you need, including coordination, delegated design and rights to the model, has to be written into the contract, because the default will not supply it.

Recall

Q. What four measures do you score your checkpoint recording on?

A. Accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, each from 1 to 5, with anything below 4 re-recorded.

Q. What happens, in concept, if someone dies without a will?

A. Default intestacy rules decide who inherits, and a court appoints an administrator. Details differ by jurisdiction.

Q. Why does a trust deed matter so much to a trustee?

A. Because the trustee's powers and duties come largely from the deed, read together with general trust law. Acting outside the deed can be a breach of trust.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a design error surfaces on site, the first question is whose error it was, and the second is what the contracts say about it. Owners often discover only then that a consultant's scope excluded the very thing that went wrong, that the liability cap is smaller than the loss, or that the owner has no right to use the model to finish the job. Every one of those outcomes was decided when the contract was signed.

The owner-consultant contract and the standard of care

In plain English, the contract with each consultant says what they will do, what they will not do, how they are paid and what happens if something goes wrong. In American practice, owners often start from published standard forms, such as those of the American Institute of Architects, the AIA, then amend them. Verify any specific form and its current edition before relying on its terms.

The central legal idea is the standard of care. In many systems, a design professional is required to perform with the skill and care ordinarily used by members of the profession in similar circumstances, not to guarantee results. Some owners try to raise that standard in the contract, for example by requiring designs fit for a stated purpose. That shifts more risk to the consultant, may conflict with the consultant's professional liability insurance, and is often resisted. Verify the legal effect where the project is located before you rely on it.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A consultant's design for a plant room ventilation system meets the code minimum but does not achieve the temperature range the owner expected, because that range was never written into the scope or the owner's project requirements. Under an ordinary standard of care, the consultant may have performed adequately. The owner's remedy was the brief, not a lawsuit. Write performance requirements into the contract documents; do not leave them as expectations.

Say that out loud now.

A consultant promises reasonable care, not a perfect building. What I need beyond that, I have to write down.

The code side: who stands behind the documents

The International Building Code, the IBC, as adopted locally, sets administrative requirements for construction documents submitted for a permit. It uses the idea of a registered design professional in responsible charge, a licensed person who coordinates the submittal documents prepared by others. It also allows certain portions of the design to be submitted later, sometimes called deferred submittals, with the building official's approval. Check the exact provisions, terms and conditions against the current adopted edition and local amendments before relying on them; I am describing the concept, not quoting a section.

This is where delegated design lives. The engineer of record may require the contractor to engage its own licensed engineer to design certain components, such as precast connections, curtain wall anchors, stair systems or fire sprinkler layouts, to performance criteria the engineer of record sets. The delegated engineer is responsible for that component; the engineer of record remains responsible for checking that it fits the overall design. Rule 98 from lesson 681 sits exactly on this boundary.

Shop drawings and submittal review

General conditions used in American practice typically say that the designer reviews shop drawings and submittals for general conformance with the design intent, and that this review does not relieve the contractor of its own responsibilities. The exact wording matters a great deal. The owner's job is to make sure the design contracts and the construction contract say the same thing about who checks what, and that changes proposed on submittals are flagged as changes.

Worked example two, hypothetical. The construction contract says the contractor is responsible for the design of all temporary works and for any substitution it proposes. The structural engineer's contract says it reviews submittals for conformance only, with no recalculation of contractor substitutions. Between them, a substituted connection is checked by nobody. The cure is one clause in each: substitutions must be identified, delegated design must be stamped by the contractor's engineer, and the engineer of record must accept the delegated calculations against stated criteria.

Coordination is a duty you have to assign

Owners often assume the architect coordinates everyone. Whether that is true depends on the contract. If the owner hires each engineer directly, the architect may have only a limited coordination duty, or none, for consultants it did not engage. The contract should say who leads coordination, who chairs model coordination meetings, who maintains the clash log and who signs the coordinated set at each gate.

A hypothetical illustration. The owner appoints the architect and, separately, the mechanical engineer, to save a markup. Neither contract assigns coordination. At construction documents, ductwork conflicts with the structural framing on several floors. The architect says the mechanical engineer was the owner's consultant; the engineer says it designed to the architect's ceiling heights. The owner pays for the redesign. One sentence in either contract would have assigned the duty and its fee.

Who owns the drawings and the model

Drawings, specifications and models are often called instruments of service. Many standard forms leave copyright with the consultant and give the owner a licence to use them for the project, sometimes conditional on payment. If a consultant is terminated, or the project is sold, the owner may need the right to use, modify and pass on the documents and the model. AIA publishes exhibits addressing digital data and building information modelling; verify the current documents before relying on them. The safe practice is to write the licence, the model's level of detail and the handover format into the contract at the start.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the uncovered loss: an error falls between scopes, the liability cap is a fraction of the loss, or the consultant's insurance does not respond to a raised standard of care. The control is to read every consultant contract against the responsibility matrix, check liability caps against realistic losses, confirm professional liability insurance in writing, and secure model and document rights at signing. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs the standard form unamended because it is standard. Standard forms are balanced starting points, written for many projects; they cannot know your scope gaps, your lender's requirements or your exit. A second mistake is assuming the permit means the design is right. A permit shows the documents were accepted for review, not that the design is free of error.

Callback

In week 78, LEX taught risk allocation: indemnities, limitation of liability and consequential loss. Consultant contracts carry the same clauses, and the same logic applies. The cap should bear some relationship to the loss a design error could realistically cause, and the insurance behind the consultant should be confirmed, not assumed.

Recap

Consultants owe reasonable care unless the contract says more. The code expects a licensed professional to stand behind the documents and allows parts of the design to be delegated or deferred. Shop drawing review is a conformance check unless stated otherwise. Secure the model and document rights at signing.

Next: Cade, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a design programme from the construction start date.
checklist: I amend standard consultant forms rather than signing them as issued.
Performance requirements are written into the contract documents.
I know what standard of care each consultant has accepted.
Delegated design items are listed, with criteria and a licensed engineer for each.
Design and construction contracts say the same thing about submittal review.
Liability caps are checked against realistic losses.
Professional liability insurance is confirmed in writing.
My licence to use the drawings and the model is secured at signing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, a design consultant usually promises reasonable professional care, not a perfect building. Anything more, such as specific performance or fitness for purpose, must be written into the contract, and raising the standard can collide with the consultant's insurance. On the code side, the IBC as adopted locally expects a registered design professional to coordinate the permit documents and allows some parts of the design to be submitted later or delegated to the contractor's own engineer; verify the exact provisions in the current adopted edition. Shop drawing review is normally a conformance check, so the design and construction contracts must agree on who checks substitutions and delegated design. Drawings and models are instruments of service; secure your licence to use and pass them on at signing. Check liability caps against realistic losses. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.
terms: Standard of care — the level of skill and care a reasonable professional in the same field would use in similar circumstances.
Delegated design — design of a specified component assigned to the contractor's own licensed engineer, to criteria set by the engineer of record.
Instruments of service — the drawings, specifications, models and other documents a design consultant produces for a project.

hostile.q: If your structural engineer makes an error, what will the project actually recover?
hostile.a: Up to the liability cap in the engineer's contract, which I have set against a realistic loss rather than accepting the default, and subject to the professional liability insurance I have confirmed in writing. Delegated components carry their own engineer and insurance. Beyond that, the project's contingency and my own risk register carry the remainder, and I can show you each figure.

title: Reverse Engineering a Design Programme From the Start Date
summary: Start from the date construction must begin and work backward through mobilisation, permit review, each design stage and each gate to find when the brief must start and when it must freeze. Then reverse engineer the clash-closure rate the model needs to reach the permit set clean.
body:
If you know when construction must start, you already know when design must start. Work backward through every stage and gate, and the date by which the brief must be written usually arrives much earlier than owners expect.

Recall

Q. What are the three decisions available at a stage gate?

A. Proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.

Q. In the currency-loss bridge, how did you find the break-even exchange rate?

A. By finding the building value in the home currency that restored the target equity, then dividing it by the building's value in its own currency.

Q. What is a fixed trust, in contrast to a discretionary one?

A. A trust in which each beneficiary's entitlement is set by the deed, so the trustee has no discretion over who receives what.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders, buyers and partners will ask when construction starts, and a confident date with no design programme behind it is a promise without a plan. This is an even week, so we reverse engineer: start from the finished outcome, the construction start, and work backward. Every figure is hypothetical; real durations depend on the project, the jurisdiction and the team, and they need confirming with your designers, your scheduler and the local authority.

The finished outcome

The construction lender's term sheet requires the contractor to receive notice to proceed in a given month. Call that week 0. Everything before it is a negative number of weeks.

Working backward, step by step

Step 1. Contractor buyout and mobilisation. The contractor needs the permit in hand and its subcontracts bought out before it can start. Allow 6 weeks. The building permit must therefore be issued by week minus 6.

Step 2. Permit review. Suppose the local authority's review, including one round of comments and resubmission, takes 12 weeks. The permit set must be submitted by week minus 18. Pricing and bidding can run in parallel with review, which is why they do not add time here.

Step 3. The construction documents gate. Allow 2 weeks for the owner's gate review, cost check and final coordination sign-off. Construction documents must be complete by week minus 20.

Step 4. Construction documents. Allow 16 weeks. They must start by week minus 36.

Step 5. The design development gate. Allow 2 weeks. Design development must be complete by week minus 38. This is also the brief freeze: after it, any change is a priced change.

Step 6. Design development. Allow 14 weeks. It must start by week minus 52.

Step 7. The schematic design gate. Allow 2 weeks. Schematic design must finish by week minus 54.

Step 8. Schematic design. Allow 10 weeks. It must start by week minus 64.

Step 9. The brief. Allow 6 weeks to write and agree the brief and the owner's project requirements, and to appoint the core consultants. The brief must start by week minus 70.

Seventy weeks is about 16 months before construction starts. The brief freeze falls at week minus 38, about nine months before start. Most owners are surprised by both numbers.

Say that out loud now.

If construction starts at week zero, my brief starts at week minus seventy and freezes at week minus thirty-eight.

Step 10. Add the float the plan does not have

The chain above has no slack. Every activity is on the critical path. One extra round of permit comments, a late survey, or a gate that sends the design back for rework will move week 0. Suppose you hold 4 weeks of owner's schedule contingency at the front. The brief now starts at week minus 74, and if nothing goes wrong you simply have 4 weeks in hand. Who owns that float, the owner or the designers, should be written down, the same principle Petra taught for construction float in week 50.

Second example: the clash-closure rate

The model is part of the programme too. Suppose the coordination report at the design development gate, week minus 38, shows 400 open significant clashes. Your rule is that the permit set at week minus 18 goes out with no open significant clashes, and that the last 2 weeks before submission are kept for final checks. So the clashes must reach zero by week minus 20.

Work backward. From week minus 36, when construction documents start, to week minus 20 is 16 weeks. The 400 existing clashes need closing at 400 divided by 16, which is 25 a week. But developing the design creates new clashes as detail is added. Suppose new ones appear at 10 a week. The team must therefore close 35 a week, gross, to reach zero on time. If the weekly coordination meeting has been closing 20, the plan is short by 15 a week, which is a signal at the gate, not at the permit counter.

What closes the gap? More coordination meetings, a dedicated coordinator, or reducing the clash count before construction documents begin by holding design development open for 2 more weeks. The last option moves the whole chain, so it must be priced against the lender's start date. That trade is the decision; the arithmetic just makes it visible.

Step 11. Check the plan against the money

Each stage also commits fees. Suppose total design fees are 2,000,000 dollars, split 15 percent at schematic, 30 percent at design development and 40 percent at construction documents, with the rest in construction. By the design development gate, 900,000 has been committed. That is the equity at risk if the project stops at that gate, which is the number Warrick's ledger asked for in lesson 682.

Step 12. Stress the programme

A backward programme should be stressed like a pro forma. Take the most uncertain duration, usually permit review, and lengthen it. Suppose review takes 16 weeks instead of 12. With 4 weeks of float in front, the start date holds, but the float is gone and any further slip moves week 0. Suppose instead the design development gate sends the mechanical design back for 3 weeks of rework. That uses 3 of the 4 weeks.

Now price a slip that the float cannot absorb. If week 0 moves by 4 weeks, the land loan, the site security, the design team's standby time and the lender's commitment all run longer. On a hypothetical 10,000,000 dollar land and predevelopment loan at 8 percent a year, four weeks of interest alone is about 62,000 dollars, before any commitment extension fee or market movement in construction prices. That number belongs beside the float, so that a decision to spend float is taken knowing what it buys.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is announcing a construction start date before working this chain backward. Once a date is in a term sheet, a pre-sale brochure or a partner agreement, every week of compression has to come from somewhere, usually from coordination quality. The control is to publish a date only after the backward programme exists, with its float stated.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner adds durations forward from today and accepts whatever date results, then tries to compress later. Work backward from the date that matters, and the plan tells you immediately whether you have started late.

Callback

In week 50, Petra taught the critical path method: the longest chain of dependent activities sets the finish date. Today's design programme is a critical path where every activity is critical. That is why stage gates must be held on time and why a gate that slips moves construction start unless float exists in front of it.

Recap

Working back from week 0: permit by minus 6, submission by minus 18, construction documents complete by minus 20, brief freeze at minus 38, brief start at minus 70, or minus 74 with float. The model needs 35 clash closures a week to reach the permit set clean.

Next: Zara, on The Room: holding the design development gate when the team wants to push on.
checklist: I work the design programme backward from the required construction start.
I confirm durations with my designers, scheduler and the local authority.
I know the date my brief must start and the date it freezes.
I hold owner's schedule contingency and state who owns it.
I know the open clash count at each gate and the closure rate required.
I compare the required closure rate with the rate actually achieved.
I know the design fees committed by each gate.
I publish a construction start date only after the backward programme exists.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, if construction must start at week zero, work backward. Allow 6 weeks for buyout and mobilisation, so the permit is needed by week minus 6. A 12-week permit review means submission by minus 18. A 2-week gate means construction documents complete by minus 20. Sixteen weeks of construction documents start at minus 36. The design development gate, which is also the brief freeze, ends at minus 38. Fourteen weeks of design development start at minus 52, ten of schematic design at minus 64, and six weeks of brief at minus 70, about 16 months out, or minus 74 with float. Then the model: 400 open clashes at the design development gate, plus 10 new ones a week, need 35 closures a week to reach a clean permit set. All of these figures are hypothetical; confirm real durations before you publish a start date.
terms: Notice to proceed — the formal instruction that allows the contractor to begin work on site.
Brief freeze — the dated point after which any change to the brief is treated as a priced change.
Clash-closure rate — the number of open model clashes resolved per week, net of new ones.

hostile.q: You have told the lender construction starts in a given month. What has to be true for that date to hold?
hostile.a: Working backward, the permit set must be submitted 18 weeks before start, construction documents finished 20 weeks before, the brief frozen 38 weeks before, and the model closing about 35 clashes a week through construction documents. We are on that programme today with 4 weeks of float in front, and I will report the gate dates and the clash count to you each month.

title: Holding the Design Development Gate
summary: At the design development gate, the architect wants to proceed to construction documents to protect the programme, but the cost estimate is over budget and the mechanical coordination is incomplete. This lesson scripts the meeting: what to say, what never to say, the question behind the pressure, when to stay silent and how to hold the gate calmly.
body:
The design development gate is the last cheap moment in the life of the building. When the team says the programme cannot afford to stop, your job is to show, calmly and with numbers, that it cannot afford not to.

Recall

Q. State Rule 98.

A. Every change to a structural element after design, including one proposed on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record as a formal, documented change with its own calculation, and nothing is built to it until that check is signed.

Q. In a meeting with a new wealth manager, what do you do after asking each custody question?

A. Stay silent and write down the answer. The first answer is usually the most honest, and vagueness under a simple question is information.

Q. What is a protector in a trust, in concept?

A. A person given specified powers over the trust, such as approving certain decisions or replacing the trustee, to add oversight. Whether and how protectors are used depends on the deed and local law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a gate is only as strong as the owner holding it. Designers are rarely wrong to want progress; their fees, their staff plans and your programme all depend on it. But a gate passed with known problems moves those problems into construction documents, where each costs several times more to fix. Holding the gate is not obstruction. It is the cheapest risk control you will ever exercise.

The scene

This is a composite example with hypothetical figures. The gate package is in. The cost consultant's estimate is 41,500,000 dollars against a budget of 40,000,000. The coordination report shows 400 open significant clashes, most between mechanical ductwork and structural framing on the typical floors. The architect, the structural engineer, the mechanical engineer, the cost consultant and Cade, who runs the model, are at the table. The architect opens: "We are tight on programme. We propose to proceed to construction documents and resolve the coordination and the cost as we go."

The lines to say

Open by restating the gate's purpose: "Thank you. The gate asks three questions: does the design meet the brief, does the cost meet the budget, and is the coordination ready for documents. We have two findings, so let us decide how to close them."

To the cost consultant: "Which three items drive most of the 1,500,000?"

To Cade: "Of the 400 clashes, how many change the floor-to-floor height or the structural grid?"

To the mechanical engineer: "If we fixed the ductwork routes on the typical floor first, how many of the 400 would that clear?"

Then the decision: "We will proceed with conditions. Construction documents begin on everything except the typical floor services, which stay in design development for two more weeks to resolve routes. The cost consultant and architect bring a costed savings list of at least 1,500,000 within four weeks. If either condition is not met, we rework."

Say that out loud now.

We will proceed with conditions. These are the conditions, these are the dates, and this is what happens if they are missed.

The lines never to say

"Just get it done." It gives up the gate and tells the team that cost and coordination are their problem, not yours.

"We will sort it out on site." It moves the cheapest fixes to the most expensive place.

"Whose fault is this?" Not in this room. Blame shuts down the information you need. Fault is a contract question for later, if ever.

"I am not technical." You do not need to be. You need the three questions and the numbers.

The question behind the question

When the architect says the programme is tight, the question behind it is often fee: staff are planned for construction documents, and a pause costs the firm money. Acknowledge it directly: "I understand a pause affects your staffing. Let us keep documents moving on everything that is ready." When the mechanical engineer says the clashes are minor, the question behind it is whether you will look closely. Cade's answer about floor-to-floor height is your test. When the cost consultant hesitates to name the drivers, the question behind it is whether bad news is welcome. Thank him for the estimate before you ask.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after asking Cade how many clashes affect height or grid. That number decides whether this is a coordination task or a design problem, and it should come from him without prompting. Stay silent after you state the conditions. The first person to speak will tell you whether the team accepts them or wants to negotiate.

Holding your state

Pressure at a gate is social. Several experts are telling you, politely, that you are slowing them down. Keep your voice low and your pace slow. Look at the gate checklist, not at the faces, when you read the findings. Remind yourself that the conditions are proportionate: most of the design proceeds; only the unready part waits. If you feel the urge to concede, ask one more question instead.

A worked moment

Cade answers: of 400 clashes, 30 would change floor-to-floor height on the typical floor. Each centimetre of height on a hypothetical 12-storey building adds façade, structure and riser length on every floor. If resolving those 30 by raising the floor-to-floor by 10 centimetres added an illustrative 400,000 dollars in façade and structure, while rerouting the ductwork within the current height cost 60,000 in extra design, the choice is easy, but only now. In construction documents the reroute is a multi-discipline reissue; on site it is not available at all.

After the meeting

The gate is not finished when the room empties. Within the day, send the gate record: the three questions, the two findings with their numbers, the decision, each condition with its owner and date, and the consequence of missing it. Ask each consultant to confirm by reply that the conditions are understood and achievable. A condition nobody confirmed is a condition nobody owns.

Then put the condition dates in your own calendar and check them on the day, not the week after. If the savings list arrives on time and totals 1,500,000, record that the condition is met and let the held work proceed. If it arrives at 900,000, the consequence you stated applies: you rework the affected areas or formally accept a revised budget with a written reason and, where required, your lender's consent. What you do not do is let a missed condition slide quietly, because the team will learn from that how much your gates mean.

Finally, tell the lender's monitor, if one is appointed, what the gate decided. Lenders prefer an owner who reports a held gate to one whose overrun appears later in a monthly report.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is passing a gate unconditionally because the programme feels more urgent than the findings. The control is the written gate record: findings, conditions, dates and the consequence of missing them, signed by you and circulated the same day.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the gate as all or nothing and, unwilling to stop everything, approves everything. Proceed with conditions exists for exactly this case. Let ready work proceed and hold back only what is not ready.

Callback

In week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern and the line "I will confirm by Friday". At a gate the owner is the one setting dates. Each condition you set is a commitment you are asking others to make, and it deserves the same discipline: specific, dated, and followed up on the day.

Recap

State the gate's three questions, take the findings with numbers, proceed with conditions where most of the design is ready, and write down the conditions, dates and consequences. Never say "just get it done" or "sort it out on site".

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: the week's six questions and a Red Pen on a consultant scope.
checklist: I restate the gate's three questions at the start.
I ask which items drive any cost overrun.
I ask how many clashes affect height or the structural grid.
I use proceed with conditions rather than all or nothing.
Each condition has an owner, a date and a consequence.
I never say just get it done or sort it out on site.
I keep blame out of the gate meeting.
I sign and circulate the gate record the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the design development gate is the last cheap moment in the life of the building. In our composite scene the estimate is 1,500,000 dollars over budget and the model shows 400 open clashes, and the architect wants to push on into construction documents. Start with the gate's three questions: brief, cost, coordination. Ask the cost consultant for the three biggest drivers. Ask Cade how many clashes change the floor-to-floor height or the grid, then stay silent. Then decide: proceed with conditions. Documents start on everything that is ready; the typical floor services stay in design development for two more weeks; a costed savings list arrives in four weeks; miss either and we rework. Never say just get it done, sort it out on site, or whose fault is this. Hear the fee pressure behind the programme argument, and sign the gate record the same day.
terms: Proceed with conditions — a gate decision that lets ready work advance while named conditions are met by stated dates.
Gate record — the written record of a gate's findings, decision, conditions, dates and consequences.
Constructability review — a review of the design by people who will build it, to find what is hard, costly or slow to construct.

hostile.q: We will lose weeks if you hold any part of the design back. Why not let us resolve coordination in construction documents?
hostile.a: Because resolving it now costs design hours, and resolving it later costs coordinated reissues across every discipline, or work on site. Most of the design proceeds today. Only the typical floor services wait two weeks, and I would rather spend two weeks now than discover in documents that thirty clashes change the floor-to-floor height. I will confirm the condition dates in writing today.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 98 Review: Managing the Design, Not Drawing It
summary: Six questions on the brief, stage gates, consultant scopes, design change control, the cost of late decisions and the backward design programme, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a consultant scope, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the owner decides what the building must be and when each decision freezes, and holds every gate, so that problems are found on paper while they are still cheap.

Recall

Q. What does clash detection do?

A. It checks a combined model of every discipline to find elements that occupy the same space or conflict, so they can be resolved before construction.

Q. What was Rule 96?

A. Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties I can verify myself.

Q. Who are the three parties to a trust?

A. The settlor, who creates it; the trustee, who holds legal title and owes duties; and the beneficiaries, who hold the benefit.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week opened the phase on designing the building. Every later week in this phase, from resilience to fire strategy to building services, sits inside the system you learned here: a brief, stages, gates, scopes and change control. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is a stage gate, and what are its three possible decisions?

Answer: A formal owner review at the end of a design stage that checks the design against the brief, the cost against the budget, the schedule and the open coordination. The decision is proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.

Question 2. What is a responsibility matrix for, and what kind of gap does it catch?

Answer: It lists every element of the building against every consultant, with one name responsible for each. It catches elements nobody designs, such as the brackets between a curtain wall and a slab edge, or firestopping at service penetrations.

Question 3. What went wrong with the Hyatt Regency walkway connection, and what is Rule 98?

Answer: A continuous hanger rod was changed on a shop drawing to two rods, so the lower walkway hung from the upper walkway's beam and roughly doubled the load on a connection that was already weak. Nobody owned recalculating the change. Rule 98: every change to a structural element after design, including one proposed on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record as a formal, documented change with its own calculation, and nothing is built to it until that check is signed.

Question 4. Why does the same design change cost more the later it is made?

Answer: Because later changes undo more work: early changes alter ideas, later ones alter coordinated drawings across disciplines and may need re-permitting, and changes on site alter built work and stop the work around them, adding schedule cost.

Question 5. What does a design consultant normally promise, and what must the owner write into the contract beyond that?

Answer: Usually the care of a reasonable professional, not a perfect result. The owner must write in performance requirements, scope and exclusions, coordination duties, delegated design rules, submittal review responsibilities, liability caps and insurance, and the licence to use the drawings and the model.

Question 6. If construction must start at week zero, how do you find when the brief must start?

Answer: Work backward through buyout and mobilisation, permit review, each gate and each design stage, adding owner's float. In the hypothetical example, that put the brief at week minus 70, or minus 74 with float, and the brief freeze at minus 38.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Zara, with Cade, built design management from the brief through stages, gates, the responsibility matrix and the owner's project requirements. Ford took the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse through seven steps, giving Rule 98 on structural changes. Sage priced the cost-of-change curve and the economics of clash detection. LEX taught the standard of care, delegated design, submittal review and rights to the model. Cade reverse engineered the design programme and the clash-closure rate from the construction start. Zara held the design development gate.

The Red Pen

Find the defects in this hypothetical extract from a mechanical engineer's scope before reading on.

Scope of Services. The Engineer shall design the heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems in accordance with applicable codes and good practice. Coordination with other disciplines will be provided as reasonably required. Equipment supports, roof penetrations and firestopping are excluded. The Engineer will review contractor submittals. Design shall be complete at Construction Documents; changes after that stage will be accommodated within the fee. The Owner may use the drawings for this project. The Engineer's liability is limited to its fee.

The defects. First, "applicable codes and good practice" states no performance requirement; without the owner's project requirements, the system only has to meet code minimums. Second, coordination "as reasonably required" assigns no lead, no meetings, no model and no clash log. Third, equipment supports, roof penetrations and firestopping are excluded with no other consultant named, which creates exactly the gaps a responsibility matrix exists to fill. Fourth, "will review contractor submittals" does not say whether the review is for conformance only or includes checking substitutions, which is where Rule 98 lives. Fifth, absorbing post-documents changes "within the fee" sounds generous but invites the engineer to resist necessary changes, and says nothing about how they are identified or approved. Sixth, the owner may use the drawings only "for this project", with no mention of the model, of modification, of use after termination, or of transfer to a buyer. Seventh, a cap equal to the fee may bear no relationship to the loss a design error could cause, and no professional liability insurance is required.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "We hire good architects and engineers. Why does the owner need to manage design at all?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because each consultant designs exactly what its contract says, and the owner is the only party who sees the whole building. We write a brief that says what the building is for and how it must perform. We hold a gate at the end of each design stage: brief, cost and coordination, and we decide proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework. We keep a responsibility matrix so no element falls between consultants. We freeze the brief at a set date, because a change costs a little at schematic stage and a great deal on site. We insist that any structural change, even on a shop drawing, comes back to the engineer of record with a calculation; the Hyatt Regency collapse is why. And we write the contracts to cover coordination, delegated design, insurance and our right to use the model. Done well, design management is the cheapest risk control on the project."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is trusting the team to manage itself because each member is competent. Competent firms working to incomplete contracts still leave gaps. The control is the owner's set of documents: brief, matrix, gate checklist and change register, maintained from the first week.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees design management as paperwork that slows design. It is the reverse. A held gate and a frozen brief are what let construction documents and construction move quickly, because the decisions behind them are already made.

Callback

In week 96, Ford's post-mortem found that personal wealth fails through its architecture more often than through its investments. A building is the same. Most design failures are not bad calculations; they are gaps in the system around the calculations: a scope nobody owned, a gate nobody held, a change nobody checked.

Recap

The owner writes the brief, holds the gates, fills the gaps between scopes, freezes decisions early, controls changes under Rule 98 and secures the contracts. Next week begins the technical design subjects, starting with resilience.

Next: Ravi, with Bram, on First Principles: resilience against flood, wind and salt air.
checklist: What is a stage gate, and what are its three possible decisions?
What is a responsibility matrix for, and what kind of gap does it catch?
What went wrong with the Hyatt Regency walkway connection, and what is Rule 98?
Why does the same design change cost more the later it is made?
What does a design consultant normally promise, and what must the owner write into the contract beyond that?
If construction must start at week zero, how do you find when the brief must start?
head: The six questions
speak: Mr Shabazz, this week's lesson is that the owner manages design without drawing it. Write a brief that states use, size, quality, budget, programme and performance. Hold a gate at the end of each stage: proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework, with a cost check every time. Keep a responsibility matrix so no element falls between consultants. Freeze the brief at a dated point, because the same change costs a little at schematic design and a great deal on site; clash detection moves changes into the model, where they are cheap. The Hyatt Regency collapse gave Rule 98: every structural change, even on a shop drawing, goes back to the engineer of record with a calculation before anything is built. Consultants promise reasonable care, so write performance, coordination, delegated design, insurance and model rights into the contracts. And work the design programme backward from the construction start.
terms: Basis of design — the design team's written explanation of how its systems will meet the owner's project requirements.
Change register — a dated log of every design change after the brief freeze, with its cost, schedule effect and approval.
Constructability — how easily, safely and economically a design can actually be built.

hostile.q: Your engineer's scope excludes firestopping and equipment supports. Who designs them on your project?
hostile.a: My responsibility matrix names the fire protection consultant for firestopping of penetrations and the structural engineer for equipment supports, with the mechanical engineer providing loads and locations. Both items were added to those scopes by amendment before design development began, and they are on the checklist for the next gate. I can show you the matrix and the amendments.
